Photograph: Bsip Sa/Alamy Cervical cancer NHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancer NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening Andrew Gregory Health editor Tue 25 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 00.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments will be offered free home testing kits on the NHS. The move comes amid concerns that only two-thirds of women attend in-person cervical screening appointments when asked to do so, leaving as many as 4 million women not up to date. The rollout is being described as a “gamechanger”, offering a “discreet and convenient option” to encourage more women to get screened. The kits contain a swab to collect a sample from the vagina. This is then posted back to the NHS free, where it is tested in labs for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). If high-risk HPV is detected, patients will then be asked to attend a cervical screening appointment with a clinician. HPV is a group of viruses that can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. About 13 high-risk types of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of cervical cancers. Starting on Tuesday, eligible women between 30 and 65 who have not attended screening appointments will be sent invitations via the NHS app, text message, email or letter. They will then be able to order a kit through the app or website. The scheme is part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040. Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS. “Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.” Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected. The latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. It means about 4 million women are not up to date, according to NHS estimates. “There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,” said Mann. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.” Athena Lamnisos, chief executive of the Eve Appeal, welcomed the move, saying that self-testing at home would be a “step-change” for many women. Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK, said: “Cervical screening is a powerful tool that saves lives – it can prevent cervical cancer or spot it at an earlier stage when treatment is more likely to be successful. “While it’s best for cervical screening to be done by a nurse or doctor, there are barriers that make it challenging for some people to attend. At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them.” Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the aim was to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. She said: “This is the future NHS we are building – there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths.” Explore more on these topics Cervical cancer Cancer NHS Health England news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

http://www.bgnes.com/economy/the-danube-.text: The dangerously low water levels of the Danube River, driven by prolonged droughts and extreme summer temperatures, have escalated from a purely environmental concern into a severe regional energy and economic crisis. Across Eastern Europe, particularly in Romania and Hungary, the shrinking river is currently severely disrupting both inland navigation and the stability of national power grids. The hydrological situation is highly complicated across the entire region. In the Bulgarian section, the water level has dropped to minus 123 centimeters below the conditional zero at the Ruse monitoring station, forcing authorities to impose strict draft restrictions on all commercial vessels and leaving ships stranded, such as the one near Belene Island. The severity of the drought is further illustrated by data from Romania, where the river's flow has plummeted to approximately 1350 to 1400 cubic meters per second. This is a drastic decline compared to the multiannual August average of 3900 cubic meters per second, highlighting the unprecedented scale of the current dry spell. This profound water shortage directly threatens the operational safety of major energy infrastructure, most notably the nuclear power plants that rely heavily on the Danube's water to cool their reactors. In Romania, the national energy company was forced to initiate a controlled shutdown of the second unit of the Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant, following the precautionary shutdown of its first unit in late July. Because Cernavoda normally provides about a fifth of Romania's manageable electricity, these shutdowns have created a significant production deficit. Consequently, the Romanian government has had to compensate by ramping up alternative sources, including hydroelectric, coal, and wind power generation, alongside relying on cross-border electricity imports. Furthermore, authorities have been compelled to urge citizens to responsibly reduce their electricity consumption during evening peak hours to prevent system overloads. Further upstream, Hungary is facing a similarly critical scenario with its Paks Nuclear Power Plant, the country's sole active nuclear facility. To prevent a complete shutdown, which would deal a devastating blow to the Hungarian economy and state budget, authorities have resorted to emergency engineering interventions. This includes the extraordinary measure of systematically sinking large barges and preparing an underwater threshold to artificially raise the water level near the plant's intake to secure the vital cooling capacity. Hungarian experts warn that if the water drops just a few more centimeters, the plant's operation could be entirely suspended. Beyond the immediate technical and logistical challenges, the crisis has sparked intense political debate regarding long-term energy strategy and climate resilience. In Hungary, Prime Minister Peter Magyar has sharply criticized his predecessor, Viktor Orban, for failing to prepare the national energy grid for these climate change-induced droughts. The lack of proactive measures over the past years, such as building adequate pumping systems or expanding alternative renewable energy sources like wind farms to compensate for nuclear shortfalls, has left the system highly vulnerable. Ultimately, the current state of the Danube underscores a critical reality for the region: the extreme vulnerability of traditional energy infrastructure to climate shifts requires immediate strategic adaptations, robust emergency planning, and a rapid diversification of energy portfolios to ensure future stability. | BGNES

https://www.dw.com/en/finland-eu-leaders.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MYM0 European leaders are in Finland to plot the increasingly important Arctic region's future Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement European leaders are gathering in Rovaniemi, Finland , on Monday to plan a path forward for the bloc's presence in the Arctic. The talks will focus on emerging shipping lanes, raw mineral deposits and security threats from the US , China and Russia . German Chancellor Friedrich Merz , Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, the prime ministers of Estonia and Latvia, the presidents of Lithuania and Romania, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and EU Council President Antonio Costa are all scheduled to attend Monday's "European Arctic Summit." "The idea is essentially to strengthen the EU's common strategic approach to the Arctic in this situation, where the geopolitical and economic significance of the region is growing considerably," according to Tuomas Tikkanen — Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's senior adviser on European affairs. Orpo, who initiated the summit, has emphasized that the Arctic is an, "increasingly important part of Europe's security environment." Finland also insists European icebreaker capabilities are included in the strategy, saying they are key to Europe's ability to operate in the High North, adding that without them it would be impossible to protect supply and trade routes, or military presence across the region. NATO drills highlight Iceland's role in Arctic defense To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video EU will use meeting to shape its new Arctic strategy No formal decisions are expected Monday, but the European Commission has said the talks will help shape its new Arctic strategy, which will be unveiled over the next few weeks. National leaders can still have a say impacting the final document, "so in that sense this is quite a timely meeting," said Finnish adviser Tikkanen. The bloc's last strategy paper was released in 2021. The Arctic, which is warming nearly four times faster than other regions, has seen increased activity as receding ice opens potential transport routes as well as access to mineral resources. That changing environment has spurred the US, China and Russia to increase energy, resource and military activity. In August, China and South Korea both sent container ships through the region, testing the viability of the North Sea Route in Russian territorial waters . Russia's Arctic buildup is Iceland's security headache To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video As Arctic ice melts, desire for control of the Arctic has heated up Although Canada, China, Russia and Scandinavian countries are all considered Arctic nations, the most concerning development of late for the EU and member state Denmark have come from an entirely unexpected corner — the United States. US President Donald Trump has threatened to blow up the NATO military alliance through his insistence that "the US must have Greenland" — a semi-autonomous island nation that is officially Danish territory — citing national security concerns, even threatening to take it by force if necessary . Trump argues that Denmark cannot protect Greenland , which is not part of the EU, from China and Russia. NATO has since launched a new security mission in the region. Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen , on a visit to Greenland, also announced closer cooperation and an investment package of €200 million ($231 million) to be used in part to set up infrastructure to extract valuable raw materials. During her visit, von der Leyen vowed that the EU would "be more engaged in Greenland and in the Arctic," saying the package would "create new opportunities and a strong and engaged EU in both Greenland and the Arctic."
